answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Top-level resource type for a DocumentDB/Cosmos account is Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the cluster/account is modelled as a databaseAccount resource).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (part of the core azure-cli distribution). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2 --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example: resource docdb 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' ... }). Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (use kind = "MongoDB" or appropriate capability block).

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical MongoDB-format connection string for the managed service: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/<dbname>?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&authSource=admin&retryWrites=false. You can also use mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/<dbname>?authSource=admin if SRV is supported. Important: TLS enabled (ssl=true or tls=true), authSource=admin, replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites often set to false.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: This managed DocumentDB offering uses provisioned compute tiers (named M-sizes such as M30, etc.) billed by vCores + storage for provisioned instances. There is also a serverless option for small workloads in some SKUs, but the primary cluster sizes are vCore-based M-tier instances (billed per vCore + storage). Not RU/s-based like CosmosDB SQL API.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary auth is MongoDB-style username/password (SCRAM-SHA-1 / SCRAM-SHA-256) where you use the account/database user and password in the connection string. The service also supports Microsoft Entra (Azure AD) identity integration in supported releases (requires obtaining an AAD access token and using the driver SASL/PLAIN or token-based mechanism supported by the server); for typical app usage you supply the Mongo credentials in the URI and use TLS. (If you plan to use Entra authentication, your app must obtain a token via azure-identity and then use the driver mechanism that accepts an access token.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB drivers (for Node.js use the official mongodb driver) and/or Mongoose for ODM in Node. There is no separate MongoDB-specific service SDK — you use standard MongoDB client libraries against the service's MongoDB-compatible endpoint.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: The service supports KNN/vector index types such as HNSW, IVF and DiskANN (exposed via the MongoDB-compatible knnVector index). Example createIndex (approximate syntax): db.interactions.createIndex({ embedding: "knnVector" }, { knnVector: { dimension: 1536, similarity: "cosine", method: { name: "hnsw", m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } })

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: For text search use MongoDB text indexes (db.col.createIndex({ field: 'text' }) and queries with {$text: {$search: '...'}}). For hybrid (text + vector) you generally combine a text-filtering pass (or attribute filters) with a knn/vector search — either server-side if the provider supports combined queries, or as a two-step approach: filter by text on the DB and then run vector nearest-neighbour ranking on the filtered set. Alternatively integrate with Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid scenarios.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: The managed service exposes the MongoDB wire protocol and commonly supports modern server version compatibility (example: MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol in current offerings). Most standard drivers for that server version work unchanged. Some server-admin or low-level features/commands (certain server-side JavaScript execution, some admin-only commands or specific storage-engine internals) may be restricted or behave differently in a managed environment; also watch for limits on transaction size and differences in consistency/latency compared to a self-hosted MongoDB.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full local emulator for this managed DocumentDB product. For local development use the official MongoDB Docker image that matches the server version (e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 mongo:7.0) and connect on port 27017. The managed cluster itself typically listens on port 10255 for TLS endpoints.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams (collection.watch()/db.watch()) are supported in the managed MongoDB-compatible service and work via the standard driver APIs. On a managed cluster nothing extra usually needs enabling, but change streams require replication internals (replica set) so the managed service must expose replica-set semantics (which it does).

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the documentdb MCP server (the 'documentdb' profile) for data-plane inspection and tooling; the general azure MCP server covers resource management but the service-specific documentdb MCP server includes the commands and tooling for inspecting collections, indexes and query plans on the managed DocumentDB cluster.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft shipped a service/API called DocumentDB which later evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. Cosmos DB provides multiple APIs (Core/SQL, MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra API, Gremlin, Table). The name DocumentDB historically refers to the older core JSON DB project; the current managed MongoDB-compatible offering is a MongoDB-compatible API hosted by Microsoft (related to Cosmos but branded for Mongo compatibility). The open-source 'DocumentDB' projects are separate and not the same as Azure's managed service.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Underneath the service is a Microsoft-managed MongoDB-compatible engine (Microsoft implements the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility). From an application perspective use standard MongoDB drivers — most application code remains unchanged. Differences to watch for: some administrative commands, limits, and operational semantics (consistency, throughput/quotas, index/feature availability) can differ from a vanilla MongoDB server.

answers.question: Which environment variable and database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Read the connection string from the DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime. Use the database name sample_healthcare_03 for all collections created and queries run by the sample.

answers.question: What Mongoose connection options and connection-string flags should the sample use when connecting?
answers.answer: Use mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }) and ensure the connection string includes authSource=admin and ssl/tls flags (e.g. mongodb://user:pass@host:10255/dbname?ssl=true&authSource=admin&replicaSet=globaldb). Do not log or persist credentials; read them from DOCUMENTDB_URI.

answers.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for nearest-neighbour search?
answers.answer: Create a knnVector index on the embedding field. Example (approximate): db.interactions.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimension: 1536, similarity: 'cosine', method: { name: 'hnsw', m: 16, efConstruction: 200 } } }). Adjust dimension to match your model (e.g. 1536 for OpenAI ada/embedding size).

answers.question: How will the agent query all pairwise interaction documents for a given list of medications?
answers.answer: Generate all unordered pairs of medications in the application and for each pair run a Mongoose query such as Interaction.findOne({ $or: [ { drugA: a, drugB: b }, { drugA: b, drugB: a } ] }). Use a normalized document shape (e.g. store drugs in sorted order) so you can query with a single equality match when possible. Use lean() for faster reads and batch queries where feasible.

answers.question: Which port and TLS settings should the sample use to connect to the managed cluster from the developer machine?
answers.answer: Connect to the managed cluster over TLS. The managed Mongo endpoint commonly uses port 10255 for TLS connections; ensure the connection string includes ssl=true or tls=true. If using mongodb+srv the SRV record will direct the client and TLS is still required.
